newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-In search for exotic, Japanese try belly dancing.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-In search for exotic, Japanese try belly dancing.

text.p: Every Friday, soon after the sun sets, strains of exotic music float out from behind the doors of a room in a rickety apartment building in the heart of Tokyo.

Throngs of young women who look like average office employees disappear behind the doors. Within minutes the apartment, actually a dance studio, bursts into colour as they change into flowing, sequined skirts, signalling the start of another belly dance class.
"I work indoors all day long and often feel the strong urge to get exercise," said Takako Fukiura, 24, a bank employee. "I have been coming here after work for the past year or so."

The undulation of bellies and wiggling of hips seen in dances originating in the Middle East is not a common scene in Japanese society. Belly dance costumes, which consist of a colourful, long skirt with a matching bikini top and veil, are even more alien.
But Karima, 37, one of Japan's few professional belly dancers and instructors says the belly dance population is slowly growing.
ALIEN BUT ENJOYABLE
"It is still far from popular and is not widely known," she said. "But compared to when I started teaching two years ago, there are definitely more people who know about it."
Karima has about 35 students now. Together with the students of the other two belly dance teachers residing in Japan, the total belly dance population would be about 100, she said.
"When I first started classes, most of the students had seen belly dancing before somewhere, either on TV or during a holiday in the Middle East," she said.

"But now, suprisingly, a lot of the girls come having no idea what it is," she said. "They arrive at the studio, try it out and stay on because they enjoy being able to do something different from others."
BANKER'S DAUGHTER LEADS THE WAY

Karima, the daughter of a banker in Yamagata, northern Japan, first started dancing as a hobby when she was studying at a university in New York. After taking lessons for about a year, she auditioned for a job at a theatre restaurant that featured a belly dance revue.
"I never dreamed of getting a part," she said. "But I somehow did and from then on I hardly went to school because I had to practise."
Less than 160 centimetres (five feet two inches) in height, Karima was the smallest dancer in the troupe besides being the only Japanese.
"The others were tall, blonde and sexy," she said, "I couldn't compete with them in terms of looks so I had to make up for it by brushing up on technique."
After a few years working as a dancer in New York, she went to Egypt and became an understudy at the Reda National Folk Dance Troupe to further her dance skills.
"I could dance, technically, but I had never really learned the intangible aspects of the art -- such as the meaning behind the various movements," she said.
"It came naturally for the Egyptians, because they had grown up listening to the songs but not for me as I had grown up in Japan."
At 52 kg (115 lb), she was considered too thin and the dancing masters did not take her seriously until her weight had edged up to 60 kg (132 lb), she said.
BREAKING STEREOTYPES

"Japanese women are petite physically and encouraged to be demure and cute," she said. "Women in Egypt are voluptuous and glamorous to begin with and when they dance, whether they are professionals or not, they do their best to show it," she said.
"Even young girls below the age of 10 shake their hips, bat eyelashes imitating adults when they dance in Egypt," she said. "In Japan, that would be considered rather precocious."
But Karima says young Japanese women are beginning to break out of the old stereotypes. Showing off their natural charms is becoming increasingly easy for them.
"I don't feel at all embarrassed about my belly button," said Miho Miyata, 26, who works at a trading house. "I kind of like being the centre of attention."
